extracted.intended_audience: Catholic catechism students / children learning basic Church doctrine
extracted.subtask_short: catechism lesson on grace and Church
extracted.subtask_description: A question-and-answer catechism lesson explaining Christian doctrines about the Church, the effects and kinds of grace, the theological virtues (faith, hope, charity), prophetic authenticity, and certain liturgical requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Four Marks of the Church
rubrics_metrics.description: "My Church will be one; it will be holy; it will be catholic; it will be apostolic; and if any church has not these four marks, you may be sure it is not My Church."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four characteristics (one, holy, catholic, apostolic) are the distinguishing signs given by Christ to identify the true Church; if any one mark is lacking the church is not the true Church. The text asserts the Roman Catholic Church is the only one that can show all four marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Church (constituent elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Church is the congregation of all those who profess the faith of Christ, partake of the same Sacraments, and are governed by their lawful pastors under one visible head."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that 'church' means the people (not the building); the congregation must profess the same faith, share the same Sacraments, and be under lawful pastoral governance with one visible head. Includes explanation of why churches/buildings are called holy (tabernacle, sacraments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Altar construction and altar stone requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: "In every altar the table, or flat part on which the priest celebrates Mass, should be of stone; but if the altar is made of wood, then at least the part just in front of the tabernacle must be of stone and large enough to hold say two chalices—about ten or twelve inches square. In this stone are placed some relics of the holy martyrs... This is called the altar stone... unless it is in the altar the priest cannot say Mass."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies material and minimum dimensions for the altar stone, the requirement to place relics of martyrs within it, the sealing/blessing ritual by the bishop, and the liturgical consequence that Mass cannot be said without the altar stone present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passover/Paschal observance ritual
rubrics_metrics.description: "God instructed Moses to tell the Israelites in the land that on a certain night they were to take a lamb in each family, kill it, and sprinkle its blood on the doorposts of their houses. They were then to cook the lamb and eat it standing, with their garments ready as for a journey. The lamb was called the paschal lamb, and was, after that, to be eaten every year... in commemoration of this event."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets out the ritual actions (select a lamb, kill it, sprinkle blood on doorposts, eat standing with garments ready) as the means by which the Israelites were spared on that night; links the paschal lamb as a figure of Christ and as an annual commemorative practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for true prophecy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Prophets are men that God inspires to tell the future. They tell what will happen often hundreds of years after their own death... True prophecy is the foretelling of something which could not be known by any means but inspiration from God."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes true prophets from statesmen and fortune-tellers: prophets speak by divine inspiration about events that could not be known naturally; fortune-tellers are sinful guessers and not prophets. It is a grave sin to consult fortune-tellers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of grace (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: "By grace I mean a supernatural gift of God bestowed on us, through the merits of Jesus Christ, for our salvation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grace is presented as supernatural (above nature), a gift not owed to us, merited by Christ's death, and intended to help the soul perform supernatural acts and obtain salvation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctifying grace
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sanctifying grace is that grace which makes the soul holy and pleasing to God."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains sanctifying grace as cleansing and purifying the soul; it restores the soul from mortal sin (bringing back its brightness) and increases holiness if the soul is only slightly stained by venial sin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual grace
rubrics_metrics.description: "Actual grace is that help of God which enlightens our mind and moves our will to shun evil and do good."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes actual grace as temporary help given for particular acts (example: a prompting to give alms or to go to Mass despite temptation). It lasts only as long as needed for the act or temptation. Examples clarify its operation and contrast with sanctifying grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacramental grace (relation to sanctifying and actual grace)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sacramental grace is sanctifying grace—given in the Sacraments—which contains for us a right to actual graces when we need them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the graces proper to each Sacrament are sanctifying in nature and that these sacramental graces entitle the recipient to subsequent actual graces aimed at fulfilling the end for which each Sacrament was instituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of grace for salvation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Grace is necessary for salvation, because without grace we can do nothing to merit Heaven."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms that human action without grace cannot attain salvation; grace is essential to perform supernatural acts and merit eternal life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human freedom to resist grace
rubrics_metrics.description: "We can and unfortunately often do resist the grace of God."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that grace is a gift which can be refused; to resist or refuse God's grace is to sin (an insult to God). This articulates moral responsibility regarding reception of grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace of perseverance
rubrics_metrics.description: "The grace of perseverance is a particular gift of God which enables us to continue in the state of grace till death."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines final perseverance (remaining in grace until death) as a gift not strictly meritable but to be prayed for; warns that one might die in mortal sin if final perseverance is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith (divine virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Faith is a divine virtue by which we firmly believe the truths which God has revealed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that faith is an infused, firm habit of belief given by God (not acquired by study); one can study to provide arguments for others, but one's faith is given by God and is equally valid whether learned young or by study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hope (divine virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Hope is a divine virtue by which we firmly trust that God will give us eternal life and the means to obtain it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies that hope concerns trust in God's promise of eternal life and in the provision of means (grace) necessary to obtain it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charity (divine virtue) and definition of neighbor
rubrics_metrics.description: "Charity is a divine virtue by which we love God above all things for His own sake, and our neighbor as ourselves for the love of God."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains charity requires loving God supremely (even above parents), and loving every human being as neighbor—'not merely the person living near us, but all men of every kind and nation—even our enemies.' 'As ourselves' means the same kind of love (not necessarily equal degree). Uses the Good Samaritan parable to illustrate who is neighbor and the rule 'Do unto others as you would have others do unto you.'
